findings.evidence: Program Overview (lines 3-8) describes what 'the people operations office' and 'IT asset group' publish, addressed to administrators. Eligibility (lines 9-15) addresses employee eligibility directly. How to Apply (lines 17-23) mixes both: employees learn about the portal, but then 'the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told' describes an internal process. The document never signals which sections are for employees versus administrators.
findings.fix: Separate content for different audiences into clearly marked sections, or add explicit audience headers (e.g., 'For Employees:' or 'For Administrators:') before each relevant passage so readers can identify which information applies to them.
findings.location: Throughout document, especially Program Overview (lines 3-8) and How to Apply section (lines 17-23)
findings.violation: The document addresses two identifiably different readers - employees applying for stipends and internal administrators - within the same sections with no clear separation, making it unclear which instructions apply to each reader.

findings.evidence: Restrictions states 'You must keep your equipment in good working condition' and 'the policy applies to one device per category.' Terminology Notes uses 'You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log.' The document never clarifies whether 'equipment,' 'item,' 'stipend item,' and 'device' are identical or distinct.
findings.fix: Choose a single term and use it consistently throughout. Define the term once in an opening glossary: 'Equipment (also called an item): the device you request reimbursement for under this stipend.' Replace all variations with the chosen term.
findings.location: Throughout document, Terminology Notes (lines 50-53) and Restrictions (lines 45-47)
findings.violation: The document uses three different terms interchangeably for what appears to be the same concept without signaling whether they are synonymous, forcing the reader to determine whether equipment, item, and stipend item refer to the same thing or different concepts.

findings.evidence: 'If the position counts as full-time, the stipend can apply. If the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, the stipend can apply. If the request arrives before the benefit year ends, the stipend can apply. Only once every condition above is met does the home-office equipment stipend become available to the employee.' The main rule (stipend availability) is stated only in the final sentence, after the reader has worked through three conditions.
findings.fix: Reorder to state the main rule first: 'You qualify for a home-office equipment stipend if you meet all three conditions: (1) your position is full-time, (2) you have completed 90 days of continuous service, and (3) you submit your request before the benefit year ends.'
findings.violation: The passage opens with three sentences of conditions before stating the governing rule, requiring the reader to accumulate three conditional statements before learning what the benefit actually is.

findings.evidence: Overview appears at both line 3 and line 59. Request Steps (lines 56-57) appears near the end, far after How to Apply (lines 17-23). Required Documentation (lines 31-35) comes after Approval Timeline (lines 25-29), forcing readers to learn what happens before they know what to send. Sections 11-13 (Program Coordination, Review Responsibility, Questions and Updates) describe internal workflows the reader does not execute.
findings.fix: Reorganize document sections to follow the reader's natural workflow: 1) Eligibility, 2) Request Steps, 3) Required Documentation, 4) How to Apply, 5) Approval Timeline, 6) Reimbursement Amounts, 7) Restrictions. Move internal process sections (Program Coordination, Review Responsibility) to a separate internal manual.
findings.violation: The document's section order does not follow the reader's task sequence. Information needed early in the process (what to document) comes after process information (timeline), critical procedural steps appear very late, and internal administrative processes are interleaved with employee instructions without separation.

findings.evidence: 36-word sentence, 4 subordinate-clause markers: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 36 words with 4 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.

findings.evidence: The document addresses employee eligibility, application procedures, internal publishing processes, administrative review workflows, equipment restrictions, compensation amounts, administrative coordination, internal review procedures, and vendor management. These six or more distinct themes lack any signal connecting them into a coherent whole. A reader completing the document cannot state whether it is primarily an employee benefits guide, an internal process manual, or both.
findings.fix: Establish a single primary purpose and audience for the document. Either create a unified employee guide focused only on what employees need to know and do, or clearly separate employee-facing sections from internal administration sections with headers and introductions explaining the division.
findings.violation: The document pursues multiple unrelated themes with no unified throughline, so a reader cannot name what the section as a whole is about.

findings.evidence: 'Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.' (line 23). The critical fact - that the backup reviewer was not informed about the sign-off requirement - is nested in the middle of the sentence. The stress position (end) contains 'before the portal releases the confirmation email,' a timing detail subordinate to the management issue.
findings.fix: Move the critical information to the stress position: 'Your review may take longer because the manager who usually handles approvals is traveling. The backup reviewer covering that absence has not been informed of the sign-off requirement, which will delay the portal's confirmation email. Please allow extra time.'
findings.violation: A critical new fact is buried in the middle of the sentence, while the stress position at the sentence's end is occupied by a subordinate technical detail.

findings.evidence: The request is reviewed within two business days.
findings.fix: Rewrite the sentence in active voice, naming the actor that performs the action.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a be-verb plus past-participle passive construction in a context where the actor is recoverable and worth naming directly.

findings.evidence: Also, the deposit happens in order to offset costs the employee already paid at this point in time.
findings.fix: Replace the wordy phrase with its plain equivalent (for example, because for due to the fact that).
findings.violation: The sentence uses a wordy construction from the fixed wordy-phrase list that a shorter equivalent would carry with no loss of meaning.

findings.evidence: However, reimbursement is not available without a completed receipt.
findings.fix: Restate the sentence with at most one negation, or recast it as a positive statement.
findings.violation: 2 negation markers from the fixed negation list co-occur in one clause, so the reader has to work out the statement's logical sign before understanding it.

findings.fix: Replace the heading with text specific enough to be found by scanning.
findings.violation: The heading text matches the fixed list of non-specific heading labels, so a reader scanning headings cannot tell whether the section applies to them.

findings.evidence: The manager approves items pursuant to internal discretion, notwithstanding the standard review checklist.
findings.fix: Replace the jargon term with a plain equivalent, or define it at first use.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a legal or foreign-language jargon term from the fixed list with no plain-language definition in the same or the following sentence.
